script.text: Good morning! I'm Kelly, and this is your daily lesson for April 16. Today we're exploring two powerful ideas together.
Look at a world map.  Greenland appears huge—almost as big as Africa.  But Africa is actually fourteen times larger.

The Mercator projection, from 1569, preserves direction—crucial for navigation. But it massively distorts size near the poles. Countries like Greenland and Canada appear enormous while equatorial regions shrink. Useful for sailors, misleading for understanding. No projection can preserve area, shape, distance, and direction simultaneously.  Every map sacrifices some accuracy for others.
Today's wisdom: Here's today's wisdom: All representations involve trade-offs.  Maps teach that every model of reality sacrifices something.
Now let's take what we learned and put it into practice.
Today's growth challenge is Map Skepticism - Question Representations.

Here's your activity: Look at a world map today—on paper or digitally. Notice how sizes and positions might differ from reality. Then consider: what other 'maps' do you rely on? Charts, graphs, summaries? What might they distort? This helps you develop awareness of how representations distort reality.
And here's how today's lessons connect: What you learned about how maps bend reality can be applied to map skepticism - question representations. Practice makes progress.
That's today's lesson. Learn something, grow a little. I'll see you tomorrow with something new. Stay curious!
